branches.theme: 1.1 Patterns All Around Us & What is Mathematics?

step_by_step_procedure: Observe regularities in daily events (calendar cycles, financial transactions, architectural tilings, leaf arrangements).
Identify repeating units or structural rules governing the arrangement.
formulas_and_identities: Pattern Rule: Sequence term T_n = f(n)
sub_branches.example_problem: Identify rule in daily calendar days: Sunday, Monday... Repeats every 7 days (Mod 7 cycle).

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Mathematics as the Search for Patterns
step_by_step_procedure: Combine artistic creativity with scientific rigor to explore structural connections.
Formulate hypotheses about why patterns occur.
Prove generalizations logically to establish universal mathematical laws.
sub_branches.example_problem: Why do consecutive odd sums form square numbers? Proved visually via L-shaped gnomons.

step_by_step_procedure: Counting numbers: Start at 1, add 1 sequentially (1, 2, 3, 4...).
Even numbers: Start at 2, add 2 sequentially (2, 4, 6, 8...).
Odd numbers: Start at 1, add 2 sequentially (1, 3, 5, 7...).
sub_branches.example_problem: Find the 15th odd number: T_15 = 2(15) - 1 = 29.

step_by_step_procedure: Powers of 2: Start at 1, multiply by 2 successively (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...).
Powers of 3: Start at 1, multiply by 3 successively (1, 3, 9, 27, 81...).
Virahānka (Fibonacci) sequence: Set V_1 = 1, V_2 = 2; add preceding two terms (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21...).
formulas_and_identities: Virahānka Recurrence: V_n = V_{n-1} + V_{n-2} (V_1 = 1, V_2 = 2)
sub_branches.example_problem: Find 7th Virahānka number: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21. Answer: 21.

branches.theme: 1.3 Visualising Number Sequences through Geometric Arrays

step_by_step_procedure: Triangular numbers: Arrange dots in equilateral triangles (1, 3, 6, 10, 15...).
Square numbers: Arrange dots in square grids (1, 4, 9, 16, 25...).
Hexagonal numbers: Arrange dots in concentric regular hexagonal rings (1, 7, 19, 37...).
sub_branches.example_problem: Calculate the 5th triangular number T_5: 5(6)/2 = 15.

step_by_step_procedure: Stack 2D square dot layers into 3D cubic prisms.
An n x n x n cube array contains n^3 dots.
sub_branches.example_problem: Find 4th cube number C_4: 4^3 = 64.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: L-Shaped Gnomon Decompositions & Sum of Odd Numbers
step_by_step_procedure: Start with a single dot (1x1 square).
Enlarge to a 2x2 square by adding an L-shaped gnomon layer of 3 dots.
Enlarge to a 3x3 square by adding a gnomon of 5 dots.
Conclude that summing the first n odd numbers equals n^2.
sub_branches.example_problem: Sum of first 12 odd numbers: 12^2 = 144.

step_by_step_procedure: Identify the central peak integer n in series 1 + 2 + ... + n + ... + 2 + 1.
Note that combining two triangles T_{n-1} and T_n with peak n forms n^2.
Take two adjacent triangular dot arrays T_{n-1} and T_n.
Align them along their diagonal boundary.
Observe that they form a complete n x n square dot grid.
Connect n points where every pair is joined by a segment (Complete Graph).
Count total connections: equals the (n-1)-th triangular number T_{n-1}.
sub_branches.example_problem: 6 people meet and everyone shakes hands once: T_5 = 5(6)/2 = 15 handshakes.

step_by_step_procedure: Start with an equilateral triangle (Iteration 0).
Replace middle third of each side with an outward equilateral triangular point.
Repeat process infinitely to generate expanding perimeter with finite area.
formulas_and_identities: Number of sides at iteration k: N_k = 3 x 4^k
sub_branches.example_problem: Find side count at 2nd iteration: 3 x 4^2 = 48 sides.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Point, Line Segment, Ray, and Infinite Line
step_by_step_procedure: Point: A precise 0-dimensional location represented by a fine dot.
Line Segment: The shortest straight path connecting two endpoints A and B (definite length AB).
Ray: Starts at endpoint A and extends infinitely in one direction (Ray AB).
Line: Extends infinitely in both opposite directions (Line AB or l).
formulas_and_identities: Line Uniqueness: Exactly 1 unique straight line passes through 2 distinct points.
sub_branches.example_problem: How many lines pass through a single point P? Answer: Infinitely many lines.

step_by_step_procedure: Intersecting lines meet at exactly one common point.
Concurrent lines are three or more lines passing through the same intersection point.
Parallel lines lie in the same plane and never intersect regardless of extension.
formulas_and_identities: Parallel Lines: Distance between lines remains constant throughout.
sub_branches.example_problem: Railway tracks represent parallel line segments.

step_by_step_procedure: An angle is formed by two rays meeting at a common vertex point O.
Angle size measures the amount of rotational divergence between the arms.
One complete rotation equals 360 degrees (360°).
formulas_and_identities: Degree Angle = Fraction of Full Turn x 360°
sub_branches.example_problem: Calculate angle for 5/12 of a full rotation: (5/12) x 360° = 150°.

step_by_step_procedure: Divide a 360° circle into N equal central spoke sectors.
Calculate central angle between adjacent spokes: 360° / N.
sub_branches.example_problem: Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes. Angle between adjacent spokes = 360° / 24 = 15°.

step_by_step_procedure: Compare angle measure theta against 90° and 180°.
Acute: 0° < theta < 90° (less than 1/4 turn).
Right: theta = 90° (exactly 1/4 turn).
Obtuse: 90° < theta < 180° (between 1/4 and 1/2 turn).
sub_branches.example_problem: Classify 125°. Answer: Obtuse Angle (90° < 125° < 180°).

step_by_step_procedure: Straight Angle: theta = 180° (exactly 1/2 turn, forming a straight line).
Reflex Angle: 180° < theta < 360° (between 1/2 and full turn).
Complete Angle: theta = 360° (full rotation).
sub_branches.example_problem: Find reflex angle corresponding to interior 70° angle: 360° - 70° = 290°.

branches.theme: 2.4 Practical Measurement using Protractor & Clock Geometry

step_by_step_procedure: Place protractor center point directly over angle vertex O.
Align one angle arm precisely along 0° baseline mark.
Read inner or outer circular scale where second arm crosses, selecting scale starting at 0°.
formulas_and_identities: Protractor Reading = Scale Mark aligned with Ray 2
sub_branches.example_problem: Ray 1 at 0°, Ray 2 at 65° on same scale => Angle = 65° (Acute).

step_by_step_procedure: Clock face has 12 equal hour divisions (30° per hour mark).
Count hour mark gap separation between hour and minute hands.
Multiply gap count by 30°.
sub_branches.example_problem: Angle at 4 o'clock: 4 gaps x 30° = 120° (Obtuse Angle).

step_by_step_procedure: Fold a straight line crease on paper directly onto itself.
Unfold to reveal a new crease line intersecting the original line at 90°.
Observe 4 adjacent right angles surrounding the intersection point.
sub_branches.example_problem: Verify paper fold perpendicularity using set-square corner.

step_by_step_procedure: Fold paper so one arm of an angle lies directly over the second arm.
Crease line formed through vertex bisects original angle into two equal halves.
sub_branches.example_problem: Bisect a 90° right angle crease. Result: Two 45° acute angles.

branches.theme: 3.1 Place Value Structure & Digit Frequency Analysis

step_by_step_procedure: Place value determines digit value by position (units, tens, hundreds...).
Calculate total count of N-digit numbers using 9 x 10^(N-1).
sub_branches.example_problem: Find total 3-digit numbers (100 to 999): 9 x 10^2 = 900 numbers.

step_by_step_procedure: Count occurrences of a specific digit separately in units place, tens place, and hundreds place.
Sum occurrences across all positional columns.
formulas_and_identities: Digit Occurrences = Sum of Positional Column Counts
sub_branches.example_problem: Count digit '7' from 1 to 100: Units place (10 times) + Tens place (10 times) = 20 occurrences.

step_by_step_procedure: A palindromic number reads identically forwards and backwards.
Symmetrical digit positions are equal (e.g., 121, 5775, 8448).
sub_branches.example_problem: Is 5775 a palindrome? Yes, 5775 reversed is 5775.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1: Take any positive integer.
Step 2: Reverse its digits.
Step 3: Add original and reversed numbers.
Step 4: If sum is palindromic, stop; else repeat steps 2-3 on new sum.
sub_branches.example_problem: Start at 48: 48 + 84 = 132; 132 + 231 = 363 (Palindrome in 2 steps).

step_by_step_procedure: Start with any positive integer n.
If n is even -> next term is n / 2.
If n is odd -> next term is 3n + 1.
Repeat until sequence reaches 1.
If a Collatz term reaches a power of 2 (2^k), it proceeds strictly by successive halving.
It reaches 1 in exactly k halving steps.
sub_branches.example_problem: Collatz sequence from 16 (2^4): 16 -> 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1 (4 steps).

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Strategic Control in the Game of 21
step_by_step_procedure: Two players add 1, 2, or 3 per turn to reach 21.
Work backward from 21 in steps of 4 (1+3=4).
Player 1 claims control numbers 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21 to guarantee victory.
sub_branches.example_problem: Player 1 starts with 1. If Player 2 adds 2, Player 1 adds 2 to reach 5.

step_by_step_procedure: Pick any 2-digit number with distinct digits.
Arrange digits descending and ascending, then subtract.
Repeat subtraction process on result to reach magic difference 9.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Raw Data vs Organized Frequency Tables
step_by_step_procedure: Raw Data: Unorganized initial list of facts or observations.
Organize raw data into categories.
Count occurrences per category to determine frequency.
formulas_and_identities: Frequency = Integer count of observations in a category
sub_branches.example_problem: Unorganized marks: 5, 8, 5, 7, 8, 5. Frequency of '5' = 3.

step_by_step_procedure: Record observations using vertical strokes '|'.
Draw 4 vertical strokes for first 4 counts ('||||').
Cross diagonally with 5th stroke to complete bundle ('||||/').
Sum bundles (5s) and individual strokes.
sub_branches.example_problem: Convert '||||/ ||||/ |||' to frequency: 5 + 5 + 3 = 13.

step_by_step_procedure: Select a simple, clear picture icon.
Declare a key scale defining how many units 1 icon represents.
Calculate icon count per category = Category Frequency / Scale Key.
formulas_and_identities: Icon Count = Category Frequency / Key Scale Unit
sub_branches.example_problem: Scale: 1 bicycle icon = 6 bikes. For 42 bikes: 42 / 6 = 7 icons.

step_by_step_procedure: Draw horizontal axis (X-axis for categories) and vertical axis (Y-axis for frequencies).
Vertical axis scale MUST start at 0.
Draw rectangular bars of uniform width.
Maintain equal spacing gaps between adjacent bars.
formulas_and_identities: Bar Height (cm) = Frequency / Quantity represented per cm
sub_branches.example_problem: Frequency = Rs 3200, Scale: 1 cm = Rs 400. Bar Height = 3200 / 400 = 8 cm.

step_by_step_procedure: Compare bar heights to identify highest/lowest categories.
Calculate category sum totals and percentage proportions.
Formulate comparative ratios.
formulas_and_identities: Category Percentage = (Category Frequency / Total Frequency) x 100
sub_branches.example_problem: Bikes = 40, Total = 90. Bike Fraction = 40/90 = 4/9.

step_by_step_procedure: Inspect vertical axis starting point.
If axis starts above 0 (truncated axis), bar height ratios distort real proportions.
Re-plot with 0-baseline to ensure visual accuracy.
sub_branches.example_problem: Bar heights of 100 and 110 look 10x taller if axis starts at 99. Fixed by starting at 0.

step_by_step_procedure: A factor divides an integer completely with zero remainder.
1 is a factor of every integer.
Every factor of N is less than or equal to N (1 <= Factor <= N).
A multiple is formed by multiplying an integer by counting numbers.
Multiples of N are infinite and greater than or equal to N.
sub_branches.example_problem: First 4 multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21, 28.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Prime vs Composite & Sieve of Eratosthenes
step_by_step_procedure: Prime Number: Has exactly 2 factors (1 and itself). 2 is smallest & only even prime.
Composite Number: Has more than 2 factors.
1 has only 1 factor -> neither prime nor composite.
Sieve of Eratosthenes: Cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7... to isolate primes.
Two integers a and b are co-prime if they share no common factors other than 1.
HCF(a, b) = 1.
sub_branches.example_problem: Are 8 and 9 co-prime? Factors(8)={1,2,4,8}, Factors(9)={1,3,9}. HCF=1 => Co-prime!

step_by_step_procedure: By 2: Last digit is even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8).
By 5: Last digit is 0 or 5.
By 10: Last digit is 0.
By 4: Last 2 digits form a number divisible by 4.
By 8: Last 3 digits form a number divisible by 8.
sub_branches.example_problem: Test 572 for 4 and 8: 72 mod 4 = 0 (Yes); 572 mod 8 = 4 (No).

step_by_step_procedure: By 3: Sum of all digits is divisible by 3.
By 9: Sum of all digits is divisible by 9.
By 6: Number is divisible by BOTH 2 and 3.
sub_branches.example_problem: Test 432 for 9: 4+3+2 = 9 mod 9 = 0 (Divisible by 9).

branches.theme: 5.4 Prime Factorisation, HCF, LCM & Fundamental Relationship

step_by_step_procedure: Decompose composite number into product of prime factors by repeated division.
Express prime factors using exponential notation.
HCF: Product of SMALLEST powers of common prime factors.
LCM: Product of GREATEST powers of all prime factors.
Multiply HCF and LCM of two numbers a and b.
Verify that product equals a x b.
formulas_and_identities: HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) = a x b

step_by_step_procedure: Perimeter is the total continuous distance around the outer boundary of a closed 2D shape.
Measured in linear units (cm, m, km).
formulas_and_identities: Perimeter = Sum of all outer side lengths
sub_branches.example_problem: Triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm: Perimeter = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 cm.

step_by_step_procedure: Rectangle: P = 2 x (length + width).
Square: P = 4 x side.
Regular Polygon with n sides: P = n x side.
sub_branches.example_problem: Regular hexagon (n=6) of side 7 cm: P = 6 x 7 = 42 cm.

step_by_step_procedure: Area measures the two-dimensional surface space enclosed within a closed boundary.
Measured in square units (sq cm, sq m, sq km).
sub_branches.example_problem: Area of room 5 m x 3 m = 15 sq m.

step_by_step_procedure: Area of Rectangle = length x width.
Area of Square = side^2.
sub_branches.example_problem: Plot 25 m long and 12 m wide: Area = 25 x 12 = 300 sq m.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Conservation of Area under Shape Rearrangement
step_by_step_procedure: Cut a shape into sub-pieces and reassemble into a new configuration.
Total area remains strictly CONSERVED (unchanged).
Perimeter can CHANGE depending on new boundary arrangement.
sub_branches.example_problem: Tangram pieces reassembled form different shapes with identical area.

step_by_step_procedure: Examine different rectangles with fixed area A.
Calculate perimeter for each rectangle configuration.
Observe that a SQUARE encloses fixed area with MINIMUM perimeter.
formulas_and_identities: Min Perimeter for fixed Area A = 4 x sqrt(A)
sub_branches.example_problem: Fixed area = 36 sq m. Rectangles: 1x36 (P=74), 2x18 (P=40), 3x12 (P=30), 4x9 (P=26), 6x6 square (P=24 Minimum).

step_by_step_procedure: Split composite L-shaped or T-shaped figure into non-overlapping simple rectangles.
Determine length and width of each sub-rectangle.
Calculate sub-rectangle areas and sum them for total area.
sub_branches.example_problem: L-shape split into 10x2 (20 sq m) and 4x2 (8 sq m): Total Area = 28 sq m.

branches.theme: 7.1 Concept of Equal Sharing & Unit Fractions

step_by_step_procedure: Divide 1 whole unit into n equal parts.
Each part represents unit fraction 1/n.
Denominator n specifies total equal parts; Numerator a specifies count of parts chosen.
sub_branches.example_problem: 3 rotis shared equally among 4 children: Each gets 3/4 roti.

step_by_step_procedure: Compare unit fractions 1/m and 1/n.
As denominator increases, individual share size DECREASES.
Proper Fraction: Numerator < Denominator (Value < 1).
Improper Fraction: Numerator >= Denominator (Value >= 1).
Mixed Fraction: Whole Integer + Proper Fraction.
formulas_and_identities: Mixed to Improper: A b/c = (A x c + b) / c
sub_branches.example_problem: Convert 3 1/4 to improper: (3 x 4 + 1) / 4 = 13/4.

step_by_step_procedure: Divide unit interval between consecutive integers into n equal sub-segments.
Count 'a' sub-segments from left to locate a/n.
sub_branches.example_problem: Locate 3/5: Divide 0-1 into 5 equal parts, mark 3rd tick from 0.

step_by_step_procedure: Multiply or divide both numerator and denominator by the same non-zero integer k.
Value remains unchanged.
formulas_and_identities: a / b = (a x k) / (b x k)
sub_branches.example_problem: Find equivalent fractions for 2/3: 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9 = 8/12.

step_by_step_procedure: When denominators are identical, add or subtract numerators directly.
Keep denominator unchanged.
Cross-multiply numerators and denominators to find common fractional unit.
Addition: a/b + c/d = (a.d + b.c) / (b.d).
Subtraction: a/b - c/d = (a.d - b.c) / (b.d).
A circle is a closed plane curve of all points equidistant from center O.
Radius r is fixed compass distance from center to boundary.
Diameter d passes through center connecting opposite points.
sub_branches.example_problem: Radius r = 4.5 cm => Diameter d = 2 x 4.5 = 9.0 cm.

step_by_step_procedure: Mark a single center point O on paper.
Set compass to radius r_1 and draw inner circle.
Without moving needle from O, adjust compass span to r_2 and draw outer circle.
formulas_and_identities: Concentric Condition: Same Center O, Different Radii r_1 != r_2
sub_branches.example_problem: Draw concentric circles with r_1 = 3 cm and r_2 = 5 cm.

step_by_step_procedure: Set compass needle at 0 mark on ruler and align pencil leg to mark length L.
Lock compass opening.
Transfer exact segment length without ruler tick parallax errors.
formulas_and_identities: Compass Span = Exact Physical Length L
sub_branches.example_problem: Transfer segment AB = 6.4 cm precisely using compass.

step_by_step_procedure: Place set-square 90° corner along baseline segment AB at vertex point.
Draw perpendicular ray along set-square vertical guide arm.
sub_branches.example_problem: Construct perpendicular ray at vertex A of base segment AB = 6 cm.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1: Draw base line segment AB = length l.
Step 2: Construct perpendicular rays at A and B using set-square.
Step 3: Mark width w along rays to locate vertices D and C.
Step 4: Join C and D to complete rectangle ABCD.
formulas_and_identities: Rectangle Construction: 4 x 90° corners, opposite equal sides
sub_branches.example_problem: Construct rectangle with length 6 cm and width 4 cm.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Inscribing Regular Hexagon using Radius Arcs
step_by_step_procedure: Draw circle of radius r.
Keep compass opening locked at radius r.
Starting at any point on boundary, step consecutive r-length arcs around circle.
Join the 6 arc intersection points to form a regular hexagon.
sub_branches.example_problem: Inscribe regular hexagon in circle of radius 4 cm. Side length = 4 cm.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Axis of Symmetry & Mirror Half Overlap
step_by_step_procedure: A figure has line symmetry if an axis divides it into two mirror-image halves.
Folding along line of symmetry causes both halves to coincide perfectly.
formulas_and_identities: Reflection Condition: Point (x, y) maps to (-x, y) across y-axis
sub_branches.example_problem: An isosceles triangle has 1 line of symmetry (vertical altitude).

step_by_step_procedure: A regular polygon with n sides has equal sides and angles.
It possesses exactly n lines of reflection symmetry.
sub_branches.example_problem: Equilateral triangle (n=3) has 3 lines; Square (n=4) has 4 lines; Regular pentagon (n=5) has 5 lines.

step_by_step_procedure: A shape has rotational symmetry if it matches its original orientation after rotation < 360° around center point O.
Order n equals total matching orientations during a full 360° turn.
formulas_and_identities: Order n = Total matching positions in 360°
sub_branches.example_problem: A 4-blade windmill matches original position 4 times in 360° (Order 4).

step_by_step_procedure: Calculate smallest rotation angle = 360° / Order n.
360° MUST be an exact integer multiple of smallest rotation angle.
sub_branches.example_problem: Square (Order 4): Smallest angle = 360° / 4 = 90°. Equilateral triangle (Order 3): 360° / 3 = 120°.

branches.theme: 9.3 Combined Symmetry in Cultural & Natural Objects

step_by_step_procedure: 24 equally spaced spokes divide 360° into 24 sectors.
Possesses 24 lines of reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry of Order 24.
Smallest angle of rotational symmetry = 360° / 24 = 15°.
sub_branches.example_problem: Rotate Ashoka Chakra by 15° -> Looks identical to original.

step_by_step_procedure: Examine non-square rectangle diagonals.
Diagonals divide rectangle into congruent triangles, BUT folding along diagonal causes vertices to overhang.
Conclude rectangle has only 2 lines of symmetry (midsegments), NOT 4.
sub_branches.example_problem: Fold rectangular sheet along diagonal: Opposite corners overhang.

mind_map.root_topic: Chapter 10: The Other Side of Zero

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Directed Quantities & Number Line Extension Below 0
step_by_step_procedure: Extend whole numbers below zero to represent opposite directed quantities.
Positive integers (+1, +2, +3...) lie right of 0.
Negative integers (-1, -2, -3...) lie left of 0.
Zero (0) is neutral (neither positive nor negative).
sub_branches.example_problem: Compare -10 and -3: -10 lies further left on number line => -10 < -3.

step_by_step_procedure: Building Lift: Upper floors (+1, +2...), Ground floor (0), Basement levels (-1, -2...).
Temperature: Above freezing (+°C), Freezing point (0°C), Below freezing (-°C).
Finance: Income/Deposit (+), Balance (0), Debt/Withdrawal (-).
sub_branches.example_problem: Lift at floor +12 moves down 15 floors: +12 - 15 = -3 (Basement level 3).

step_by_step_procedure: The additive inverse of an integer a is -a.
Adding a number and its additive inverse yields zero.
sub_branches.example_problem: Additive inverse of +15 is -15 because (+15) + (-15) = 0.

step_by_step_procedure: Adding a positive integer -> Move RIGHT on number line.
Adding a negative integer -> Move LEFT on number line.
Subtracting a positive integer -> Move LEFT on number line.
Subtracting a negative integer -> Move RIGHT on number line.
formulas_and_identities: a + (+b) = Right b; a + (-b) = Left b; a - (-b) = Right b
sub_branches.example_problem: Evaluate 2 + (-5): Start at 2, move 5 units left => Reaches -3.

step_by_step_procedure: Represent positive numbers with green (+1) tokens and negative numbers with red (-1) tokens.
Pair one green and one red token to form zero-pairs (+1 + -1 = 0) and cancel out.
Count remaining uncancelled tokens for net result.
sub_branches.example_problem: Evaluate -8 + 13: 8 red tokens cancel with 8 green tokens; 5 green tokens remain => +5.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Algebraic Rule for Subtracting Negative Integers
step_by_step_procedure: Subtracting a negative integer is equivalent to adding its positive opposite.
Change double negative '- (-b)' to '+ b'.

branches.theme: 10.4 Brahmagupta's Laws of Zero & Integer Arithmetic

step_by_step_procedure: Brahmagupta (628 CE, Brahmasphutasiddhanta) defined formal laws for zero and negative numbers.
Law 1: A - A = 0.
Law 2: A - 0 = A.
Law 3: 0 - A = -A.
sub_branches.example_problem: Apply Brahmagupta's Law 4: 0 - (-7) = +7.

sub_branches.concept_or_rule: Multi-step Integer Expressions & Real-World Word Problems
step_by_step_procedure: Set up mathematical expression with correct signs for gains (+), drops (-), deposits (+), and withdrawals (-).
Evaluate systematically from left to right using operational rules.
formulas_and_identities: Net Position = Initial + Sum of Changes
sub_branches.example_problem: Submarine at -250 m dives 120 m deeper (-120 m) then ascends 180 m (+180 m): -250 - 120 + 180 = -190 m (190 m below sea level).
